strengths: The core method is simple, well-motivated, and clearly described: fine-tuning only the diagonal blocks of selected weight matrices, with an equivalence shown between the block-diagonal adapter D and directly updating the diagonal blocks of W (g_Di = g_Wii).
The gradient analysis (Section 3.2) cleanly explains why DiaBlo avoids the vanishing/unstable gradient issues of the AB low-rank product, and the zero-initialization argument is sound.

Computation cost analysis (Section 4.5) correctly shows that DiaBlo and LoRA have the same forward/backward FLOPs and parameter count when N*d^2 = 2mr, and the runtime benchmark (Table 6) empirically confirms parity with LoRA.

Evaluation is broad: commonsense reasoning (FP16 and BF16), arithmetic reasoning, code generation, safety alignment, and 4-bit/2-bit quantized fine-tuning, across Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B, and Mistral-7B, with results consistently at or above strong PEFT baselines like DoRA, PiSSA, MiLoRA, SMT, and LoRI.
Hyperparameters and implementation details are provided in the appendix, and code is stated to be released, supporting reproducibility.
The quantized-model experiments (Table 5) are a nice addition, showing DiaBlo outperforms specialized quantized-finetuning methods (LoftQ, ApiQ) without any customized quantization machinery.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and incomplete positioning: block-diagonal / structured diagonal fine-tuning has been explored before (e.g., SVFT [32], FLoRA, BdLoRA, DeloRA), yet the paper compares only against SMT among structure-based methods and cites SVFT without comparing to it. Missing these direct competitors weakens the 'novel PEFT framework' claim.

No empirical memory measurements are reported despite repeated claims of 'comparable memory efficiency' to LoRA; Table 6 reports only wall-clock time. Since DiaBlo's adapter parameters live in FP32 within the model, an actual memory comparison is needed to support this headline claim.

The 'more stable convergence' claim is asserted but never demonstrated: there are no loss curves, gradient-norm analyses, or variance across seeds; all results appear to be single-run numbers without error bars or significance tests.

Baseline results are largely copied from prior papers (DoRA, MiLoRA, SMT, LoRI, ApiQ) rather than re-run under a unified setup, which risks inconsistencies in hyperparameter tuning; the paper's own learning rates differ substantially across models/settings, raising fairness questions.

Ablations are thin: no study of sensitivity to block size N beyond two values, no analysis of which module types (Q/K/V vs Up/Down vs O/G) matter most, and no experiment on tasks where the diagonal-block subspace might underperform low-rank updates (the 'Low-Rank vs. Full-Rank' discussion is purely anecdotal).
The 'geometric interpretation' paragraph (Section 1) is hand-wavy and not substantiated by any analysis or experiments.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'DiaBlo consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance among PEFT approaches' when on some benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval Pass@1 vs. LoRI) it merely 'closely matches' baselines, and in Table 3 the N=64 setting trails full fine-tuning on average.

strengths: The proposed method (DiaBlo) is simple, easy to implement, and integrates into standard training pipelines without specialized initialization or optimizers, which is a genuine practical advantage.

The equivalence between the block-diagonal adapter D and directly fine-tuning the diagonal blocks of W (Section 3.2) is stated cleanly, and the einsum-based implementation makes the method efficient in practice.

Experiments cover several task families (commonsense reasoning, arithmetic reasoning, code generation, safety alignment, and quantized models) across multiple model families (Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B), and hyperparameter details are provided in the appendix.
The efficiency analysis (Section 4.5) and runtime benchmark against LoRA and DoRA are a useful addition, showing DiaBlo matches LoRA's training speed.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: tuning structured subsets of pretrained weights is well explored (SMT, SVFT, block-diagonal variants of LoRA such as FLoRA/BD-LoRA-style decompositions). The core idea—train a small number of full-rank sub-blocks of W—is a natural simplification of these ideas, and the paper does not adequately position DiaBlo against or differentiate it from the closest prior work.

The theoretical content is thin. The gradient analysis only shows the obvious fact that training D equals training the diagonal blocks of W, and the 'geometric interpretation' in the introduction (sheared, anisotropically rescaled plane) is hand-wavy and never formalized or tested. No analysis of why the diagonal-block subspace should be better than other block placements.

Missing critical ablations and controls: (i) a comparison with randomly selected (non-diagonal) blocks of the same parameter budget to test whether diagonality matters at all; (ii) sensitivity to the choice of N; (iii) which modules to adapt. Without these, the central design choice is not validated.

Unfair or loosely controlled baselines: several baseline results are copied from other papers (DoRA, MiLoRA, SMT, LoRI, ApiQ) rather than re-run, potentially under different tuning budgets; in Tables 2 and 4 DiaBlo uses notably more trainable parameters than LoRI (1.51% vs 0.56%), yet is declared to 'surpass' baselines. Parameter-matched comparisons are inconsistent across tables.
No error bars, seeds, or statistical significance; many reported gaps (e.g., 83.5 vs 83.4, 87.3 vs 87.2, 88.0 vs 87.9) are within typical run-to-run variance for 8-task averages.

Memory efficiency claims are not substantiated: Section 4.5 argues theoretical equivalence with LoRA but reports only wall-clock time in Table 6; no peak GPU memory measurements are given, despite 'memory and computational efficiency' being a headline contribution.

The abstract claims DiaBlo 'consistently outperforms existing PEFT methods,' but on code generation (Table 4) LoRI clearly outperforms DiaBlo on Llama3-8B unless an extra training epoch is added (42.65 vs 43.2), a detail that undercuts the strong claims.

Reproducibility and polish issues: the code URL in the abstract is dangling ('Codes are available at' with no link), Appendix A.1 contains a duplicated/erroneous sentence ('hyper-parameters for FP16 are provided in 7 and ... for FP16 are provided in 8'), and there are multiple typos (e.g., 'we may expand the pad the weight W', 'Ma teusz Litwin').

Motivation is somewhat overstated: the paper frames LoRA's difficulty as stemming from low-rank matrix products being non-convex, but LoRA with zero-init B is generally well-behaved in practice; the claimed stability benefit of DiaBlo is asserted rather than demonstrated (e.g., no convergence curves or gradient statistics are shown).

strengths: The proposed method is remarkably simple: fine-tuning only diagonal blocks of selected weight matrices, initialized to zero. This avoids the matrix-product structure of LoRA and eliminates the need for special initialization or optimization tricks, which is an appealing design choice.

The paper provides a clean and correct analysis showing that the gradient of the block-diagonal adapter D_i equals the gradient of the corresponding diagonal block of W (g_D_i = g_W_ii), establishing equivalence to fine-tuning diagonal blocks of the original weights, and contrast this with the entangled gradients of LoRA's A/B factors.

The empirical evaluation is broad and thorough: commonsense reasoning (FP16 and BF16), arithmetic reasoning (GSM8K/MATH), code generation (HumanEval), safety alignment (HEx-PHI), and quantized fine-tuning (4-bit and 2-bit), across LLaMA2-7B, LLaMA3-8B, and Mistral-7B. DiaBlo is competitive or superior to strong recent baselines (DoRA, PiSSA, MiLoRA, SMT, LoRI, ApiQ) at comparable or smaller parameter budgets.
The efficiency claims are supported both theoretically (same parameter count and FLOPs as LoRA when matched) and empirically (Table 6: runtime matches LoRA at 170 min vs. DoRA's 480 min).
The paper is clearly written, the method is easy to implement (einsum-based batched matmuls), and hyperparameter details are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. Structured/sparse weight-subset fine-tuning is well explored (e.g., SMT for sparse sub-matrices, SVFT for singular-vector updates, and prior diagonal/block-diagonal + low-rank approaches such as Zhang & Pilanci's diagonal+low-rank PEFT, which is not discussed). The paper's positioning against this closely related line of work is incomplete, weakening the claim of a genuinely new PEFT direction.

The theoretical justification is thin. Beyond the trivial gradient equivalence, there is no analysis of why the diagonal-block subspace is sufficient, no expressivity results, and the 'geometric interpretation' in the introduction (sheared, anisotropically rescaled region) is hand-wavy and not rigorously connected to the experiments.

Memory efficiency is claimed but never directly measured; only runtime (Table 6) is reported. Since DiaBlo's trainable blocks live in FP32 alongside FP16 frozen weights like LoRA's adapters, actual GPU memory comparisons would strengthen the central efficiency claim.

Results are reported without multiple seeds or variance estimates, and several headline improvements over baselines are small (e.g., 83.5 vs. 83.4 for SMT on Llama2-7B; 88.3 vs. 87.2 for LoRI on Llama3-8B BF16), making statistical significance unclear.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'consistently outperforms existing PEFT methods' is not fully supported (e.g., LoRI clearly beats DiaBlo on HumanEval Pass@1 for Llama3-8B, and DiaBlo needs an extra training epoch to match it); on code generation the advantage is mixed.
The code availability link in the abstract is incomplete ('Codes are available at' with no URL), which hurts reproducibility as submitted.

Sensitivity to the number of blocks N is explored only at two values (64, 128); a more complete ablation of N, module selection (Q/K/V/Up/Down), and interaction with model size would better characterize the method.

Experiments are restricted to 7-8B language models; there is no evidence the conclusions extend to larger models or other modalities (acknowledged in Limitations, but this narrows the significance of the findings).

strengths: The core idea—fine-tuning only the diagonal blocks of weight matrices—is simple, well-motivated, and easy to implement, avoiding the matrix-product parameterization and initialization sensitivity of LoRA.

The paper provides two theoretical results: DiaBlo-LSQ solutions match full least-squares solutions under a rank condition (Theorem 1), and DiaBlo stationary points coincide with stationary points of full fine-tuning when activations/output gradients are low-rank (Theorem 2), with empirical validation of the low-rank assumptions (Appendix A.2).

The empirical evaluation is broad: commonsense reasoning, arithmetic reasoning, code generation, safety alignment, quantized (4-bit/2-bit) fine-tuning, MT-Bench, and GLUE, across multiple models (Llama2-7B/13B, Llama3-8B, Mistral-7B, T5-base).

A useful ablation (Table 5) shows diagonal blocks are a better-structured sparse pattern than random entries/blocks/rows/columns, both for retaining fine-tuned updates and for direct sparse fine-tuning.

Reasonable efficiency analysis showing DiaBlo matches LoRA's theoretical compute/memory at equal parameter counts, with measured training speed (170 vs 480 min/epoch vs DoRA) and hyperparameter/learning-rate sensitivity studies (Tables 10, Figures 5-6).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: block-structured and band-structured PEFT already exists (e.g., block-diagonal LoRA variants, BA-LoRA (Tian et al., ICLR 2025), S2FT's structured sparsity). DiaBlo is essentially the special case of updating only diagonal blocks, yet the closest works like BA-LoRA and block-diagonal adapter families are not discussed or compared, weakening the claimed positioning.

Comparisons are not always at matched parameter budgets, which inflates apparent advantages: e.g., in Table 3 DiaBlo uses 1.51%/0.76% trainable parameters vs LoRI's 0.56%; in Table 1 DiaBlo (1.04%) has more parameters than LoRA/DoRA (0.83%). 'Outperforming' claims at larger budgets are less meaningful.

Many baseline numbers are copied from other papers (DoRA, MiLoRA, SMT, LoRI, ApiQ) under possibly different training/hardware settings rather than re-run under a controlled protocol, raising fairness and comparability concerns.

No error bars, seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported for any result; several headline margins (e.g., 83.5 vs 83.4 vs SMT's 83.4 on Llama2-7B; 87.3 vs 87.2 vs SMT on Llama3-8B) are within plausible noise, so 'consistently outperforms' is overstated.

Theoretical claims are stronger than what is proven: Theorem 2 only guarantees that DiaBlo's stationary points are stationary points of full FT (not convergence, not optimality); the 'strictly more expressive than LoRA' claim holds only in the linear least-squares setting with specific rank conditions, yet the abstract/general framing suggests more generality.

Some results are inconsistent with the narrative: on arithmetic reasoning, DiaBlo with the more parameter-efficient N=64 setting (42.1) underperforms full FT (43.2), and DiaBlo N=32 requires more parameters (2.09%) than LoRA r=64 (1.67%) to win; such caveats are not clearly discussed.

Writing and presentation issues: broken/citation-free code link ('Codes are available at .'), typos ('very cloes', 'DiaBlo permit', 'less number'), a truncated sentence at the end of the related-work paragraph on page 2, and repeated references (Wang et al., 2024c/d are the same paper).
Reproducibility is partially undermined: the code repository link is missing in the manuscript, and some experiments rely on reproducing settings described only in other papers' codebases.

strengths: The proposed method (DiaBlo) is simple, easy to implement, and integrates into standard training pipelines without specialized initialization or optimizers.

The empirical coverage is broad: commonsense reasoning, arithmetic reasoning, code generation, safety alignment, quantized models (4-bit/2-bit), GLUE, MT-Bench, plus ablations on block count N, learning rates, layer-wise sensitivity, and sparse-pattern comparisons.

The paper provides some theoretical analysis (Theorems 1 and 2) relating block-diagonal updates to full fine-tuning under low-rank conditions, and empirically verifies the low-rank assumptions and gradient alignment in Appendix A.2.
The implementation uses batched einsum operations, and the efficiency analysis (memory/throughput vs. LoRA and DoRA) is a useful practical contribution.
Hyperparameter details are provided in the appendix, and the experimental protocol largely follows prior work (MiLoRA, LoRI, LoRA-GA settings), aiding comparability.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea — fine-tuning a small structured subset (blocks) of existing weight matrices — is very close to existing structured-sparsity PEFT methods such as S2FT (Yang et al., 2024a), SVFT, and random-block adaptation. The main delta is restricting blocks to the diagonal, and the paper does not convincingly articulate why the diagonal placement per se is the key ingredient rather than block-structured updates in general. Table 5's gaps over random-block fine-tuning are small (67.68 vs 64.86 on GSM8K), and no variance or significance testing is reported anywhere; all results appear to be single runs.

Evidence for superiority is mixed and sometimes weakens the claims: in Table 3, DiaBlo uses 1.51% trainable parameters versus LoRI's 0.56% and only matches its Pass@1 (43.2 vs 43.2), and on Mistral-7B the code-generation improvements over LoRA are marginal. In Table 1, DiaBlo's advantage over SMT(best) on Llama3-8B is 0.1 points. The headline claims of 'consistently outperforms' are stronger than the evidence.

Theoretical results have limited practical bite: Theorem 1 requires X to be a generic rank-r matrix with N <= m1/r, and Theorem 2's stationarity guarantee relies on a 'genericity' assumption plus low-rank activations/gradients; the argument that DiaBlo is 'strictly more expressive than LoRA under the same parameter budget' is confined to the linear least-squares setting and does not establish anything about the nonlinear fine-tuning regime where the method is actually used.

Reproducibility is undermined: the code link in both the abstract and the Reproducibility section is empty ('Codes are available at .'), so the stated artifact is not actually provided. No seeds or confidence intervals are reported for any benchmark.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top-tier venue: broken citation 'GPT, 2023' and '(Hayou et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2021)' for LoRA; mangled reference entries (e.g., 'OpenAI Josh Achiam', pervasive raw Semantic Scholar URLs); typos ('cloes', 'a less number of trainable parameters'); an incomplete sentence ending 'S^2FT...' in Section 1; and a reference list that duplicates entries (Wang et al., 2024c/d).

The efficiency argument that DiaBlo has 'the same theoretical computational cost as LoRA at equal trainable parameters' glosses over practical realities: DiaBlo's dense-block pattern means updating d x d blocks rather than thin rank-r factors, and the claimed parity is asserted rather than rigorously benchmarked across shapes; memory comparisons to baselines at matched parameter budgets are not systematically reported.

Several key design choices are under-justified: why diagonal (rather than arbitrary block positions, which Table 5 suggests perform close to diagonal), how N should be chosen for a new model/task beyond '64 or 128 work well', and whether the method interacts well with modules where m1 != m2 (e.g., attention Q/K/V in grouped-query architectures) is only superficially addressed.

strengths: The proposed method is simple, well-motivated, and easy to implement: directly updating diagonal blocks avoids the matrix-product parameterization of LoRA and the associated initialization/optimization sensitivities, which is a practically appealing contribution.

The paper provides theoretical grounding: Theorem 1 (DiaBlo matches full LSQ minimizers under low-rank inputs, with a parameter-efficiency comparison to LoRA) and Theorem 2 (stationarity of the full FT objective under low-rank activations/gradients) are supported by complete proofs, and the assumptions are empirically validated (Appendix A.2).

Evaluation is broad and largely convincing: commonsense reasoning, arithmetic reasoning, code generation, safety alignment, quantized (4-bit/2-bit) fine-tuning, GLUE, and MT-Bench, across multiple model families and scales, with competitive or superior results to LoRA, DoRA, PiSSA, MiLoRA, SMT, LoRI, and quantized-PEFT baselines.

Useful ablations and analyses: comparison of diagonal blocks vs. random sparsity patterns (Table 5), ablation over the number of blocks N (Table 10), learning-rate sensitivity (Figure 5), gradient-norm stability analysis (Table 9), layer-wise sensitivity (Figure 7), and module-selection experiments (Figure 6).

Good reproducibility practices: hyperparameters for all experiments are documented, model sources listed, and code is stated to be released; the efficiency analysis (Section 4.5) gives both a theoretical complexity argument and measured wall-clock comparisons.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: fine-tuning structured sub-blocks of weight matrices has been explored (e.g., S2FT's structured sparsity, block-diagonal/band structured adapters, and related masked-submatrix approaches). The paper does not clearly distinguish DiaBlo from the closest prior block-diagonal-structured PEFT work, which weakens the claim of a fundamentally new direction.

Some headline comparisons use different trainable-parameter budgets (e.g., DiaBlo N=64 uses 1.04% parameters vs. 0.83% for LoRA/DoRA in Table 1), and in several tables DiaBlo needs more parameters than the strongest baselines to win, which partially undercuts the 'more efficient' narrative; parameter-matched comparisons should be foregrounded more carefully.

Many baseline numbers are taken from prior papers (DoRA, MiLoRA, SMT, LoRI, ApiQ, LoRA-GA) rather than re-run under identical settings, so cross-table comparability is not fully guaranteed; no variance over random seeds is reported for the main results.

The theoretical results, while correct and cleanly presented, are relatively direct linear-algebra arguments (genericity + low-rankness), and the stationarity guarantee is weaker than global-optimality guarantees for the nonlinear setting; the 'converges to a stationary point of full FT' phrasing in the abstract could be read as stronger than what is proven.

Presentation issues: the code repository URL is missing ('available at .' on page 1 and in the reproducibility statement); the 'GPT, 2023' reference is nonstandard; a few typos ('cloes', 'permits a larger numbers of blocks', 'a less number of trainable parameters').

The stability claims rest largely on gradient-norm variance statistics over three epochs on one model/task; more direct evidence (e.g., performance variance across seeds) would better substantiate the central stability argument against LoRA.
